Staging

The prognosis of invasive breast carcinoma (IBC) is influenced heavily by the overall TNM stage as assessed by pathology (pTNM) based on the staging systems of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017. ]] and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) {28094848}, with excellent survival in early-stage disease and decreasing survival rates with increased stage at diagnosis {25585328}.

The pathological assessment of tumour size / local extent (pT) and regional lymph node status (pN) is essential and standard to both staging systems. Distant metastatic spread classification (pM) is primarily determined by the results of radiological studies, with pathological confirmation after biopsy in some cases.

The pTNM staging factors are combined to define five anatomical stage groupings (0, I, II, III, and IV) with implications for both prognosis and clinical management (see #51747Table 3.03). Of note, modifiers to the stage are used in specific scenarios, such as the “y” prefix for post–neoadjuvant treated cancer specimens and the “m” prefix for specimens with multiple separate foci of invasion.

In addition to the traditional anatomical stage, the eighth edition of the AJCC staging system created a complementary prognostic stage grouping system that incorporates anatomical TNM information with tumour-intrinsic biology, including the Nottingham grade and biomarkers (ER, PR, ERBB2 [HER2]), in addition to multigene assays in the ER-positive subgroup of patients when available {28294295;28094848}. The prognostic stage is typically assigned by the clinical team once all pathology testing is complete. This system has been shown to improve stratification of patients with respect to outcome.

Size assessment

pT stage classification relies on appropriate initial gross examination and tissue sampling. Gross skin changes such as ulceration and satellite skin nodules, and inflammatory changes such as redness and dimpling should be noted and correlated with clinical findings because pT4 disease status is defined by gross and clinical rather than microscopic findings. pTmi and pT1–3 IBCs are categorized based on pathology assessment of tumour size. Small invasive cancers (especially those < 5 mm) are often best evaluated by measuring the microscopic size present on a single tissue section. However, for larger tumours, the correlation of gross, microscopic (from composite sections or multiple sequential slices), and imaging findings is often necessary to determine the best pT category. Whole tumour size is a non-core recommended reporting element used in the International Collaboration on Cancer Reporting (ICCR) dataset, including ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or pleomorphic lobular carcinoma in situ extending beyond the invasive cancer, which may help correlate with the overall imaging extent {38719547} [[International Collaboration on Cancer Reporting (ICCR) Internet. Sydney (Australia): ICCR; 2025. Available from: http://www.iccr-cancer.org. ]]. However, it is invasive tumour size that determines pT (for additional information on gross tissue sampling for determination of pT stage, see Macroscopic appearance in section Epithelial tumours of the breast: Part 2: Introduction).

Post-neoadjuvant evaluation of residual cancer burden/size estimations is discussed below (see Neoadjuvant therapy response).

Lymph node assessment

Lymph node stage is one of the most important pathological factors to determine the stage, prognosis, and subsequent management of breast cancer (BC). Axillary surgery is associated with significant morbidity, including lymphoedema and sensory and motor nerve issues, and there is increasing evidence for de-escalation {25992218;28139362;36383926;37495945;38598571;33810544} and even omission {37733364} of axillary lymph node surgery in a range of settings. There is level 1 evidence that sampling the first draining or sentinel lymph nodes for pathological assessment results in accurate staging, and this approach can be used to obviate the need for axillary dissection {28838210}.

Lymph nodes can be assessed clinically (as part of pretreatment staging and decision-making) and pathologically. Detailed methods of the pathological assessment of surgically removed ipsilateral lymph nodes for BC is available in the ICCR dataset {36270029}. Lymph nodes should be evaluated in 2 mm slices, to identify all macrometastases (metastases > 2 mm). Metastatic deposits ≤ 2 mm but > 0.2 mm (or > 200 cells) in a lymph node are known as micrometastases and define the case as node-positive (pN1mi), whereas cases with only isolated tumour cells (< 0.2 mm) are considered node-negative (pN0i+) for staging purposes {36270029}.

Immunohistochemistry is not usually required in the pathological evaluation of axillary lymph nodes, but it may be used to clarify the nature of suspicious or atypical cells in some cases (e.g. lobular carcinoma or post-neoadjuvant cases). Intraoperative frozen section or imprint cytology has reasonable sensitivity for preliminary evaluation of lymph node status to determine the need for further axillary staging during initial surgery, or decisions on axillary dissection can be deferred to permanent sections {23953247;27900818;20439323;24899463;29649327}.

Post-neoadjuvant evaluation of axillary lymph nodes is discussed below (see Neoadjuvant therapy response).

Histological grading

IBCs are graded using the Nottingham grading system, which correlates with prognosis and other histopathological features and biomarker status {18490649}. Three characteristics are evaluated: tubule formation as an expression of glandular differentiation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic count {1757079;20804570}. A numerical scoring system from 1 to 3 is used to ensure that each factor is assessed independently.

Tubules and gland/acini formation are assessed throughout the whole tumour at low magnification; only structures exhibiting clear central lumina surrounded by polarized neoplastic cells are counted. Cut-off points of 75% and 10% of glandular/tumour area are used to determine the score. These rules also apply to tumours with simple gland/tubule formation such as invasive tubular carcinoma, and those exhibiting complex gland formations such as invasive cribriform carcinoma. Larger islands of tumour with central gland formation, as may be seen in mucinous carcinoma or invasive micropapillary tumours, can be regarded as tubule formation for grading purposes (although these may represent central cisterns rather than true gland formation and data is limited on this topic) {38719547} [[International Collaboration on Cancer Reporting (ICCR) Internet. Sydney (Australia): ICCR; 2025. Available from: http://www.iccr-cancer.org. ]]. Papillary structures are not regarded as glandular/tubular structures, and neither is intracytoplasmic lumen formation, whatever the size of the intracytoplasmic vacuoles.

Nuclear pleomorphism is assessed in the area with the highest degree of pleomorphism in comparison with the regularity of the nuclear size and shape of normal epithelial cells in adjacent breast tissue. The preferred magnification for nuclear scoring is the 40× objective. Increasing irregularity of nuclear outlines and the number and size of nucleoli are useful additional features in allocating scores for pleomorphism. Score 1 nuclei are very similar in size to the nuclei of benign pre-existing epithelial cells (< 1.5 times the size), and they show minimal pleomorphism, an even chromatin pattern, and nucleoli that are either not visible or very inconspicuous. Score 2 nuclei are larger (1.5–2 times the size of benign epithelial cell nuclei), with mild to moderate pleomorphism and visible but small and inconspicuous nucleoli. Score 3 nuclei are even larger (> 2 times the size of benign epithelial cell nuclei), with vesicular chromatin; they vary markedly in size and shape and often show prominent nucleoli. The minimum proportion of tumour nuclei which should show marked nuclear atypia/pleomorphism before a score of 3 is allocated has not been well defined, but the finding of an occasional enlarged or bizarre nucleus should not be used to give a score of 3 rather than a score of 2.

The evaluation of mitotic figures requires care and relies on optimal tissue fixation and good preparation of sections. Observers must count only definite mitotic figures; hyperchromatic and pyknotic nuclei should be ignored because they are more likely to represent apoptosis than cells in mitosis. Mitotic counts require standardization to a fixed field area, because field area varies between microscopes. The total number of mitoses per 10 HPF is recorded. The cut-off points for scoring depend on the field area size, and the microscope used should be calibrated by measuring the diameter of the HPF (40× objective). Scoring is performed on the area exhibiting the highest frequency of mitotic figures (the hotspot method), typically the peripheral leading edge of the tumour. If there is heterogeneity, regions exhibiting a higher frequency of mitoses should be chosen. Once the hotspot is chosen and the first field is considered, subsequent field selection is by random meander through the chosen area, but only fields with a representative tumour-cell burden should be assessed. The cut-off points for the number of mitoses identified in a tumour area of 2 mm2 is mitotic score 1 at ≤ 7, mitotic score 2 at 8–14, and mitotic score 3 at ≥ 15 (see #48123Table 1.01 in section General introduction on score thresholds for mitotic counts based on the diameter of the HPF and its corresponding area). When using a digital pathology system, it is recommended that one or more fields with a tumour-assessed field area of 2 mm2 are used {34556501}.

The three grading values are added together to produce a score of 3–9, to which grades are assigned as follows: 3–5 points = grade 1, well differentiated; 6–7 points = grade 2, moderately differentiated; and 8–9 points = grade 3, poorly differentiated. For the purpose of quality assurance, it is recommended that the individual score components be reported in addition to the calculated grade (see #51747Table 3.03).

The grading of small tissue samples, such as core needle biopsy specimens, is possible and often necessary in the era of neoadjuvant treatment, but it should be recognized to have limitations, in particular owing to the inherent reduced ability to accurately assess mitotic frequency. This may lead to underestimation of the true grade in such specimens {20557310}.

With the emergence of digital pathology, there have been recent efforts to utilize deep learning methodology for the subtyping of BCs using digitized H&E slides for the quantitation of histological features, such as mitotic index and nuclear features (i.e. offering either a diagnostic aid for grading or a unique digital grade). The reproducibility of mitosis counting may be improved in accuracy and concordance using artificial intelligence (AI) {32622359}. Recent studies have demonstrated that grade 2 BCs could be stratified into clinically meaningful groups using an algorithm based on an ensemble of convolutional neural network models {38831336}. An AI approach also offers the potential for a rapid and cost-effective alternative to molecular-based assays using H&E-stained sections with AI-based tools that have the capability of risk stratification {39143539}. While AI has the potential for improved accuracy, efficiency, and standardization, work flow considerations, data requirements, algorithm validation, and regulatory issues need to be addressed prior to implementation.

Lymphovascular invasion

The pathological diagnosis of lymphovascular invasion (LVI) is based on Rosen’s histopathological criteria {6674861}. LVI is defined as tumour emboli within peritumoural vascular channels (lymphatics and capillaries) outside the main tumour mass. Therefore LVI should only be assessed in surgical specimens at the borders of invasive carcinoma, rather than in intratumoural specimens, and only in vessels clearly lined by endothelial cells, with awareness of retraction artefacts that may cause a false positive assessment. LVI is positively associated with high tumour grade, large tumour size, and positive nodal status. It is an independent prognostic factor of local recurrence and poor survival in all subtypes of early BC {22180017;38771398}. The extent of LVI is often used for determination of postsurgical radiotherapy indications; however, there are not well validated definitions of extensive LVI. LVI is considered extensive if it is present in more than two blocks, although the data to support this is limited [[Fitzgibbons PL, Bose S, Chen YY, et al. Protocol for the Examination of Specimens from Patients with Invasive Carcinoma of the Breast. InvasiveBreast 4.1.0.0. Northfield (IL): College of American Pathologists; 2018 Jan. Available from: https://documents.cap.org/protocols/cp-breast-invasive-18protocol-4100.pdf. ]].

LVI does not impact T staging; however, it is important to report the presence of dermal LVI because of its strong association with the clinical diagnosis of inflammatory BC.

Retraction artefacts are the major pitfall in the interpretation of LVI. Immunohistochemistry with D2-40 and antibodies against CD31 and ERG can be used for confirmation, but caution should be used owing to potential cross-reactivity with stroma cells or false negative staining {20133078;18206495}. Myoepithelial markers can also be useful to distinguish from DCIS with retraction.

Surgical margins

Accurate margin-status evaluation depends on appropriate specimen orientation by the surgeon (using designated sutures, staples, or inks) and subsequent annotation at grossing with various inks before gross dissection (if not done by the surgeon), followed by sectioning and tissue sampling such that potentially close margins can be evaluated histologically. The distance from each close margin should be measured histologically and reported. When surgeons take additional shave margins, these are considered the final true margins and supersede the corresponding margins of the initial surgical specimen. Most guidelines endorse a “no invasive tumour at ink” margin for IBC and a 2 mm margin for DCIS (when it is not associated with invasion) to reduce local recurrence risk {27528719;24521674;24473640;12433599}. The location and extent of positive/close margin involvement should be noted for both invasive carcinoma and DCIS. Various recommendations for reporting of surgical margins are available {32442067;38719547;35869801;27528719} [[Fitzgibbons PL, Bose S, Chen YY, et al. Protocol for the Examination of Specimens from Patients with Invasive Carcinoma of the Breast. InvasiveBreast 4.1.0.0. Northfield (IL): College of American Pathologists; 2018 Jan. Available from: https://documents.cap.org/protocols/cp-breast-invasive-18protocol-4100.pdf. ]].

Neoadjuvant therapy response

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is frequently used in the setting of triple-negative, HER2-positive, and some high-risk hormone receptor–positive BCs. Treatment response is a powerful prognostic measure of residual risk of recurrence, which informs if additional therapies may be indicated to further reduce this risk. Cancers with a complete pathological response have an excellent prognosis, and this has been used in clinical trials testing new regimens as an early surrogate for overall survival {30516102;28564564}. A complete pathological response to treatment (defined most often as no residual invasion in the breast or lymph nodes) is most common in hormone receptor–negative cancers. For those that do not achieve a complete pathological response, an estimation of the residual disease burden can be of clinical utility and prognostic relevance. Neoadjuvant endocrine therapy may be administered to patients with ER-positive IBC in certain clinical scenarios.

One clinically validated method for the pathology evaluation of post–neoadjuvant chemotherapy surgical specimens is the residual cancer burden (RCB) [[University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center Internet. Houston (TX): University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center; 2025. Residual cancer burden calculator. Available from: http://www3.mdanderson.org/app/medcalc/index.cfm?pagename=jsconvert3. ]] {17785706;34902335}, which utilizes a thorough gross tumour-bed sampling strategy to map out the extent of residual disease in the breast. The RCB system uses the span and cellularity of the residual cancer (with estimations of the percentage of carcinoma in situ subtracted from the total), as well as number of lymph nodes with residual cancer and largest metastatic lymph node focus, to determine an RCB score and class. The RCB is supplementary to post-neoadjuvant ypTNM stage, which uses different size-measurement criteria. In contrast to the most commonly used staging systems, those of UICC and the AJCC, which use the largest contiguous focus of invasion for ypT stage, RCB uses the overall span of invasion foci present within the fibrous tumour bed/scar. This difference is also true of size estimates of the largest metastatic deposit in an axillary lymph node.

RCB is recommended to be included as a reporting element or as an optional reporting element for post-neoadjuvant IBC in reporting guidelines. The ICCR has a dataset for post-neoadjuvant BC reporting recommendations {38443320}. Other recommendations also exist, such as those of the Residual Disease Characterization Working Group of the Breast International Group–North American Breast Cancer Group collaboration {26205180}.

Histological changes in the residual cancer after neoadjuvant therapy are variable. Therapy-resistant cancers may have minimal to no change, while cancers with treatment effect may display either small nuclei and minimal cytoplasm or bizarre cells with large, irregular nuclei and vacuolated cytoplasm. The mitotic count is often lower in the residual carcinoma, and as a result the histological grade of the treated carcinoma may differ from that of the core biopsy. There is limited evidence for prognostic relevance of histological grade after neoadjuvant treatment, but guidelines recommend it should be reported using standard Nottingham grade {38443320;39580878}. In rare cases, the only residual cancer is in lymphatic spaces, which has been associated with worse survival outcomes and is not regarded as a complete pathological response {18936689;29394169}. In this scenario, the RCB span of the residual invasion could be measured using the span of the LVI in two dimensions {38443320}.

After a complete response, the treated tumour bed often displays loose, oedematous, vascularized fibroelastotic stroma with chronic inflammatory cells, macrophages, and haemosiderin deposition. This area may also contain foreign body reaction evoked by marker clips inserted before/during treatment. In the event of a complete pathological response, a comment regarding the presence of tumour-bed changes and/or clip site should be included in the report to indicate that the correct area has been examined histologically {38443320}. When only small foci of atypical cells are present, immunohistochemical studies may be helpful for distinguishing cancer cells from benign histiocytes or reactive myofibroblasts, and invasive carcinoma from carcinoma in situ. DCIS may be present in the absence of invasive carcinoma (ypTis) and is still considered a complete pathological response, and these patients have a favourable prognosis {24529560}.

Primary neoadjuvant endocrine therapy is sometimes administered but rarely results in a complete pathological response. Treated cancers may have a central area of fibrous scarring and often the IBC cells are smaller than before treatment and are less proliferative {17650216}. While the RCB is not used in the setting of post-neoendocrine treatment, the span of residual invasion and cellularity may be reported to describe treatment response.

Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes

Quantitative assessment of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) on standard H&E-stained slides has been strongly associated with survival outcomes and response to systemic therapy and immunotherapy, particularly in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), HER2-positive breast cancer, and high-grade hormone receptor–positive breast cancer {34311075;39838118}. High TIL levels correlate with greater rates of complete pathological response in TNBC and HER2-positive and high-grade hormone receptor–positive disease. TNBCs with higher levels of baseline TIL levels are prognostic of improved overall survival, even in the absence of systemic treatment {38563834;31566659}. Higher TIL levels are also associated with PDL1 positivity and a greater magnitude of benefit with the addition of immunotherapy, and when both PDL1 is positive and TIL levels are high, these immune-rich tumours are especially responsive to immunotherapy {34311075}.

Numerous studies have utilized samples from prospective clinical trials to provide high-level evidence (level of evidence 1B) supporting the prognostic and predictive capabilities of TILs as a biomarker. While currently not standard practice at all sites, morphological TIL assessment can be incorporated into pathology reports as a routine prognostic factor, akin to tumour size, grade, or nodal status. TIL scoring has been standardized by the International Immuno-Oncology Biomarker Working Group on Breast Cancer, which is available in more detail online (www.tilsinbreastcancer.org). Broader adoption of TIL assessment, including computationally assessed TILs, may potentially refine therapeutic precision and prognostic estimates and reduce treatment-related toxicities {32411818;37608772}.

Biomarkers and predictive molecular assays

Biomarkers are used for prediction of benefit from specific therapies and for prognostic purposes to determine the need for treatment escalation versus de-escalation in BC. Hormone receptor (ER and PR) status and HER2 status are recognized as indispensable predictive and prognostic factors for IBC therapy decision-making in international guidelines published by the St. Gallen International Breast Cancer Expert Panel {29733336;28838210}, the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) {23970019}, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) {20586616;24099077}, and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) {28404755} [[National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN). NCCN clinical practice guidelines in oncology (NCCN guidelines): breast cancer. Version 1.2025. Fort Washington (PA): NCCN; 2025. Available from: https://www.nccn.org/professionals/physician_gls/default.aspx. ]].

Core biopsies are preferred for ER, PR, and HER2 testing because they have short ischaemic times and better fixation than surgical specimens. However, if the resection specimen has a different tumour type in terms of morphology or grade, a new test may be advisable to rule out heterogeneity in biomarker expression. Standardized BC biomarker reporting templates are available [[College of American Pathologists Internet. Northfield (IL): College of American Pathologists; 2025. Cancer Protocol Templates cited 2025 Jul 2. Available from: https://www.cap.org/protocols-and-guidelines/cancer-reporting-tools/cancer-protocol-templates. ]]. Laboratories and pathologists assessing ER, PR, and HER2 should participate in external quality assurance processes to ensure the accuracy of results.

Additional single biomarkers and multigene assays have relevance restricted to specific settings, such as PDL1 testing in triple-negative metastatic BC, and the 21-gene recurrence score assay in early-stage ER-positive BCs. The most commonly utilized biomarkers are reviewed in the following sections.

Estrogen receptor

Evaluation of all new primary or metastatic IBCs for evidence of nuclear ER expression by immunohistochemistry is recommended because of its utility in predicting clinical benefit from endocrine therapy and its use in various clinical treatment algorithms for ER-positive versus ER-negative cancers. ER expression helps define prognostic stage groups, and can be used as a surrogate for luminal versus non-luminal intrinsic subtype classification as defined by gene expression. Most ER-positive, luminal-type BCs have uniform and diffuse ER expression with > 90% of nuclei staining; however, a smaller percentage will have more variable or focal weak staining {15762275}.

Most guideline recommendations for immunohistochemistry testing of ER and PR in BC state that BCs with as few as 1% of cells with weak intensity of ER staining should be considered positive, because of evidence of potential benefit from endocrine therapy {31928404}. However, because of more limited evidence in the small group of cancers with ER expression levels just above the 1% threshold, invasive cancers with 1–10% ER positivity should be reported as “ER low positive” with a standardized comment that states these limitations (see #51689Table 3.04) {31928404}. An accumulation of data from this small and heterogeneous group suggests that the clinical and histopathological features of ER low positive cancers are often more similar to ER-negative cancers {28712925;37684569;22291085;34251757}. This should be considered in decision-making for other adjuvant therapy and overall treatment pathway / classification.

Because of the importance of ER immunohistochemistry testing as a predictive and prognostic marker in BC, test validation and quality assurance standards are essential. In daily practice, an external control should always be evaluated (with a range of appropriately positive and negative tissues), and internal controls should also stain as expected when present. The status of internal controls should be reported for cases with 0–10% staining and negative cases. For cases with these results without internal controls present and with positive external controls, an additional report comment is recommended, suggesting to test another specimen with internal controls to confirm the result. See the most recent versions of the guidelines for up-to-date information about test interpretation {31928404}.

Progesterone receptor

Within the group of cancers that are ER-positive, the percentage of cells with nuclear PR expression, seen on immunohistochemistry, is considered a prognostic marker: cases with lower PR expression levels are associated with worse outcomes, but patients may still receive benefit from endocrine therapy if ER-positive {15272277;24675287;27722840;27044936;24325948;31928404;24300977}. Specific PR thresholds for prognostication are not well validated {36653923;28532429}. According to guidelines, cancers with ≥ 1% of cells with PR positivity are considered PR-positive.

PR expression in the absence of detectable ER is rare and since PR expression is induced by ER, this has mostly been attributed to false negative ER or false positive PR status. There is poor reproducibility of this ER-negative, PR-positive group across different ER clones and there is debate about its significance {35397755;27125355;29772460;38178166;26363528;23233704}.

HER2

In 10–20% of IBCs, the ERBB2 gene is amplified, resulting in overexpression of the HER2 protein at the cell surface. This protein overexpression can then result in the promotion of more-aggressive cancer biology due to increases in cancer proliferation, cell motility, and angiogenesis.

HER2 overexpression/amplification is considered both a predictive and a prognostic biomarker in BC. HER2 is a marker of aggressive biology and poor prognosis in the absence of appropriate therapies. A positive HER2 test is predictive of survival benefit when HER2-targeted therapies are added to chemotherapy regimens. Therefore, a HER2-positive test makes a patient a candidate for chemotherapy in combination with various HER2-targeted therapies. In the post-neoadjuvant setting, HER2-positive BCs that do not achieve a complete pathological response may be treated with additional novel HER2 antibody–drug conjugate treatment. Treatment in the metastatic setting is rapidly evolving, with specific HER2-targeted antibody–drug conjugate options now approved in both HER2 overexpressed/amplified cancers and metastatic cancers with lower levels of expression (termed “HER2 low and ultralow” in clinical trials) {35665782;39282896}. HER2 protein status is assessed using immunohistochemistry and ERBB2 gene amplification is assessed by in situ hybridization (ISH). Detailed test performance and interpretation recommendations are available in country-specific guidelines {29846122;29846104;36564170}.

Because immunohistochemistry is readily available, and lower in cost, many laboratories use it as the first test performed; if there is an equivocal result (2+ staining), the case is automatically referred for ISH testing (either in-house or at a reference laboratory). HER2 testing guidelines recommend using immunohistochemistry to inform the final HER2 status of unusual ISH categories {29846122;29846104}.

The evaluation of membrane stain intensity is critical to the appropriate determination of HER2 immunohistochemistry score as immunohistochemistry 0, 1+, 2+, or 3+. Overinterpretation of 2+ stain intensity as 3+ is one of the most common causes of discordance between HER2 immunohistochemistry (positive) and in situ hybridization (negative) {20660333}. The comparison of stain intensity with controls that include the range of expression should serve as a reference for intensity measures. A practical approach is to use the magnification rule, which takes into account the magnification of the lens required to assess the staining, as follows: using a 10× ocular, if staining is noted with a 2–5× objective, it can be considered strong intensity; staining detected using a 10–20× objective is considered weak to moderate; and staining detectable only on 40× magnification is considered faint / barely perceptible. Interpreters should be aware of unusual staining patterns (e.g. clustered heterogeneity) and discordant results (e.g. grade 1 cancer with 3+ HER2 staining) (see #51688Table 3.05) {29413654}.

The DESTINY-Breast04 and DESTINY-Breast06 trials have changed the clinical relevance of lower levels of HER2 expression on immunohistochemistry, making it important to pay attention to the discrimination of cases with no HER2 expression at all (0 / absent membrane staining) from cases with any membrane staining, such that patients with metastatic disease who are eligible for treatment with the antibody–drug conjugate trastuzumab deruxtecan can be identified {35665782;39282896}. In these trials, standard American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) / College of American Pathologists (CAP) HER2 scoring was used, and “HER2 low” was considered immunohistochemistry score 1+ or 2+ / ISH negative, and “HER2 ultra low” was immunohistochemistry score 0 with membrane staining that is incomplete and faint / barely perceptible in < 10% of tumour cells (0+ / with membrane staining). Patients with no membrane staining (0 / absent membrane staining) were not eligible for DESTINY-Breast04 and DESTINY-Breast06, so it is still not clear if low-level HER2 immunohistochemistry expression is predictive of response to treatment. The smaller DAISY trial included patients with immunohistochemistry 0 with evidence suggesting they were also responsive to trastuzumab deruxtecan {37488289}. This may be explained if samples with no immunohistochemistry expression are false negative results, with HER2 protein levels either below the limit of detection of the assay or affected by preanalytical or analytic factors {35595825;35113131;39970411}. Current testing guidelines and consensus statements on HER2 low address best practices to aid in recognition of these subtle low-level staining differences and reporting standards {37284804;37269905;37770765}. Details of the semiquantitative immunohistochemistry scores, including specifying the specific staining pattern in immunohistochemistry 0 cases (e.g. 0 / absent membrane staining vs 0+ / with membrane staining), are recommended, but reporting using HER2 low and ultralow terminology is not required.

Proliferation marker Ki-67

Proliferation rate can be useful as a correlate and adjunct to Nottingham grade in BCs, potentially adding useful information about how fast the cancer is growing and its possible susceptibility to agents that might disrupt the cell cycle (e.g. chemotherapy and cell-cycle inhibitors). Reductions in proliferation rate have also been used as an indicator of response to neoadjuvant treatments. Proliferation rate is particularly relevant in determining which ER-positive, HER2-negative BCs might need treatment beyond endocrine therapy {33369635}. While a range of gene expression panel-based assays using sets of proliferation-related genes are routinely used to assist in treatment decision-making in luminal BC, these assays are expensive, limiting equitable global access {34461263}.

Ki-67 is one of the most widely used proliferation markers. It is a nuclear protein present during all active phases of the cell cycle and absent in resting cells. While it does generally correlate with mitotic counts, there are discrepancies {26379080}.

While there have been significant concerns about reproducibility of the assay, the International Ki67 in Breast Cancer Working Group (IKWG) has undertaken numerous studies and has developed validated guidelines and training for immunohistochemistry scoring, which is available at https://www.Ki-67inbreastcancerwg.org. The IKWG recommends that cut-off points of ≤ 5% (low) and ≥ 30% (high) can be used to estimate prognosis in ER-positive, HER2-negative stage I/II BC {33369635}. However, there is poor reproducibility in the 10–20% range.

Similarly to other BC biomarkers performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues, such as ER, PR {31928354}, and HER2 {29846122}, preanalytical factors can impact the reliability of Ki-67. A significant difference in Ki-67 counts between core biopsy and matched resection specimens was demonstrated {35729220}, probably due to preanalytical factors including fixation and specimen handling. Therefore, Ki-67 is best assessed on core biopsy. Appropriate quality control should be undertaken and participation in quality assurance programmes is recommended {33369635}.

Markers relevant to immune-checkpoint therapy

ICIs have transformed cancer treatment across various tumour types, including BC. They are currently part of the standard of care in early and advanced TNBC, with emerging evidence of their efficacy in the ER-positive/HER2-negative setting {38521654;37003065}. However, most testing for these markers is currently only relevant in the metastatic setting.

PDL1, a transmembrane immune-checkpoint protein expressed on tumour cells and immune cells, is a key biomarker for ICIs. PDL1 immunohistochemistry assessment presents challenges owing to different platforms, antibodies, and scoring systems showing suboptimal concordance {33580222}. Currently, the combined positive score (CPS) is the only clinically used scoring system in BC, with CPS ≥ 10 an indication for pembrolizumab in metastatic TNBC. CPS is the ratio of the number of PDL1-positive cells, including tumour cells and immune cells, divided by the number of viable tumour cells, multiplied by 100 {37003065}.

Tumour mutation burden and microsatellite instability / deficient mismatch repair are also testing options in the metastatic setting that may determine eligibility for ICIs; however, BCs with a high tumour mutation burden and high microsatellite instability are rare {22318517;32067680;32019858;32461104;34606929}.

The evolving utility of immune gene signatures has also shown promise, in their ability to predict response to ICIs in a variety of settings {30557521;34638323}.

Androgen receptor

AR testing in IBC for predictive or prognostic purposes is not standard practice and there are no guidelines that define a clear cut-off for its positivity. Therapies targeting AR are not part of routine practice in BC, but there is interest in the potential use of antiandrogen therapy in TNBCs with AR expression {39833837}.

Gene expression profiles

Although ER-positive, HER2-negative BC is regarded as biologically less aggressive, it accounts for about 60% of all BC deaths owing to its persistent recurrence risk beyond 5 years {29117498}. Several analytically and clinically validated gene expression assays providing prognostic information for distant recurrence risk in ER-positive, HER2-negative early BC treated with adjuvant endocrine therapy have been developed {34461263}. The 21-gene recurrence score (RS) and a 70-gene assay have been evaluated in prospective, randomized trials providing level 1A evidence supporting their intended use (TAILORx in node-negative and RxPONDER in 1–3 positive axillary nodes for the 21-gene RS, and MINDACT in women with clinically high-risk disease and ≤ 3 positive axillary nodes for the 70-gene assay) {29860917;34914339;27557300}. These assays can identify women with low genomic risk who do not benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy (see #56401Table 3.06) {34082017}. Algorithms that combine prognostic information provided by the 21-gene RS and clinicopathological features give more prognostic information than either alone {33306425;39621968}. For example, the implications of 21-gene RS for premenopausal versus postmenopausal patients is different depending on specific RS and lymph node status.

Molecular therapeutic targets, ESR1, PIK3CA, AKT1

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumour suppressor genes involved in DNA repair through homologous recombination {12470990}. In individuals with mutations in the BRCA1/BRCA2 genes or other genes involved in homologous recombination DNA repair (PALB2, ATM, ATR, CHEK2), this mechanism is impaired and unable to fix the double-strand DNA breaks induced by PARP inhibitors, leading to synthetic lethality {15829967}.

In early-stage BC, PIK3CA mutations appear in 32% of patients and are linked with ER positivity, increased age, lower tumour grade, and smaller tumour size {29470143}. There are PI3K inhibitors available for patients with PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic BC progressing on hormonal therapy. Other alterations of this pathway include AKT mutations and PTEN loss, which result in uncontrolled AKT/mTOR signalling. These are also more commonly found in luminal cancers and the metastatic setting, with a frequency of 3–13% {32213086}.

ERBB2 activating mutations are present in about 5% of BCs, with higher frequencies in invasive lobular carcinoma {32213086}. These mutations occur independently of HER2 amplification status and are found in both HER2-positive and HER2-negative tumours.

ESR1 encodes ER-α, a ligand-activated transcription factor present in approximately 75% of IBCs {15318928}. ESR1 mutations – the most common being NM_000125.4:c.1613A>G p.(Asp538Gly), NM_000125.4:c.1610A>C p.(Tyr537Ser), and NM_000125.4:c.1609T>A p.(Tyr537Asn) – often occur in the ligand-binding domain of ER, leading to constitutive activation of the receptor independent of estrogen. This results in continued proliferation of cancer cells despite the use of aromatase inhibitors and selective estrogen receptor modulators {27986707;24185512}. Their prevalence is very low in untreated primary BC (< 1%), but they are enriched (up to 30–40%) after treatment with an aromatase inhibitor, especially in the metastatic setting of ER-positive BC and can be detected in peripheral blood samples / liquid biopsy {26560360;26122181}.

Liquid biopsy is a broad concept encompassing the detection and analysis of circulating nucleic acids (circulating cell-free DNA and circulating tumour DNA), circulating tumour cells, exosomes, immune cells, circulating proteins, and other tumour-derived products. Circulating tumour DNA is composed of a mix of DNA released by the many different tumour subclones, better capturing cancer heterogeneity.

The clinical applications of these circulating biomarkers range from their use for early detection of cancer or relapse, staging and monitoring of patients with localized or advanced cancer, monitoring the efficacy of therapies, tracking tumour evolution, and identifying resistance mechanisms {35809752;26969689}.

Liquid biopsies can be used to detect recurrent somatic mutations in oncogenes clustered in hotspots, such as acquired ESR1 mutations in the ligand-binding domain (i.e. Tyr537, Asp538, and Glu380) {26560360}. In the metastatic ER-positive BC setting, detection of ESR1 mutation by a blood sample is the preferred method of determining if acquired resistance has developed to traditional hormone receptor treatments and the potential benefit of switching to a specific oral selective ER degrader {37196213}. Liquid biopsies can also identify PIK3CA mutations, which are actionable with PI3K inhibitors {31091374}.

Prognostic/predictive assays in limited-resource settings

The availability of BC immunohistochemical and molecular predictive tests for ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67 in limited-resource settings may be reduced owing to multiple factors, including the affordability of these tests, lack of specialist diagnostic centres, expensive quality assurance programmes in anatomical pathology, and shortages of pathologist staff. In sub-Saharan Africa, there is approximately 1 anatomical pathologist per 1 000 000 people, whereas in high-income settings the ratio is closer to 1 per 15 000–20 000 people {29550029}.

Centralized specialized diagnostic centres where complex testing can be performed may be available in some settings, allowing for quality testing of standard BC biomarkers such as ER and HER2. However, higher-cost predictive testing typically used to determine if chemotherapy is needed in ER-positive BCs, such as the 21-gene assay, may not be available. No-cost alternatives are an option in these settings, such as the refined Magee Equations, which use pathological parameters (Nottingham grading score, Ki-67 proportion score, tumour size, and H scores for ER, PR, and HER2 status) to predict the 21-gene RS in invasive BC {36165933}. Additionally, the Magee Decision Algorithm uses the results of the Magee Equations and the mitotic count to triage cases that might benefit from sending these tests to reference laboratories {30395177}. A recent review reports that the Ki-67 index can also be used as an alternate strategy to the 21-gene RS to predict the likelihood of recurrence in hormone receptor–positive early BC {38779417}.

Although still nascent, adoption of digital pathology and AI-based tools has the potential to overcome the shortage of skilled pathology workforce in these settings. AI tools for primary BC diagnosis, grading of BC, counting mitoses, TIL enumeration in TNBC for prognostic information, prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response, and more-recent prediction of molecular signatures can make predictive and prognostic testing accessible in low-resource settings {38388367}.
